newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's Hail Ck coal mine back on track.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's Hail Ck coal mine back on track.

text.p: Mining group RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd is pressing ahead with development plans for one of the long-awaited giants of the Australian coal industry, the A$500 million Hail Creek mine in central Queensland.

The project, proposed in the 1970s in the first wave of big opencut coal projects in Queensland, is back on CRA's active list and has just completed a formal presentation in Tokyo to the Japanese steel mills, partners in the venture told Reuters.
Despite some apparent misgivings and hedging by the Japanese steel mills, Hail Creek is now scheduled to begin large-scale mining at the rate of five million tonnes a year in 2000.

Hail Creek is owned 69 percent by CRA Ltd unit Pacific Coal Ltd, 25 percent by Exxon Corp subsidiary Esso Australia Resources, four percent by Japan's Marubeni Corp trading house and two percent by Sumitomo Corp.

Hail Creek was on the verge of going ahead in the 1970s but was left on the back-burner while other big Queensland coal projects proceeded amid simmering warfare between the Australian Labor government and the Japanese steel mills over coal pricing.
Sumitomo Metal Australia Pty Ltd's managing director Kazuo Tanimizu told Reuters Hail Creek now will begin production at five million tonnes a year in 2000.
The project's prospects were affected by a short-term bearish outlook for thermal coal, he said.
While thermal coal was very bullish in the long-term, many new mines coming onto the market had produced a temporary excess of supply over demand, he said.
Infrastructure problems, including rail links, also remained to be solved, he said.
"(But) we're still going ahead very positively," he said.

According to Tokyo trade reports, a presentation by Pacific Coal to the Japanese steel mills depicted Hail Creek as producing 60 percent coking coal, 30 percent semi-soft coking coal and 10 percent thermal coal.
Japanese buyers also harbour some reservations over the marketability of segments of Hail Creek's coal, they said.
Japan's biggest steelmaker, Nippon Steel Corp, was considering bringing Hail Creek to life in the near-term at one million tonnes a year, according to the reports.
Tanimizu said problems of lower-scale production and of environmental approval caused a "soft" start-up option to be scrapped.
RTZ-CRA officials were not immediately available for comment.
